The Lighthouse at Harrow Point

The lighthouse at Harrow Point was built in 1847 to warn ships away from a reef that had already claimed forty vessels. Its keepers lived on the rock for months at a time. They trimmed the lamp, polished the lens, and logged the weather every four hours.

Supplies arrived by boat when the sea allowed it. In winter the crossing could be impossible for weeks. The keepers learned to ration flour, oil and patience in equal measure. One logbook records a December in which the only visitor was a stray gull.

Automation arrived in 1974. A small controller replaced the nightly watch, and the last keeper left the island that spring. The lens still turns today. It is checked twice a year by a technician who describes the visit as the quietest day of his job.

Visitors now climb the 112 steps to the gallery on summer weekends. From the top, the reef is visible as a pale line under the water. Guides explain how the light was once measured in candlepower. They also explain why that measure was retired.

Local historians have collected the keepers' logbooks into a single archive. The entries are brief and practical. They mention storms, repairs, and the occasional birthday. Read together, they form a surprisingly warm record of a lonely trade.

Plans to turn the keeper's cottage into a museum were approved last year. Work begins in March, once the nesting season ends. The first exhibit will be the lamp itself, lit for one evening so that visitors can see it as the sailors did.
